# Results — Study 398 (Entropy-Efficiency)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The **"efficiency clock"** —
the claim that when the market's **entropy drops** (returns become more ordered / predictable)
a tradable window opens — tested on SPY. We compute a causal **rolling permutation entropy**
of daily returns (Bandt-Pompe, 60-day window, embedding m=3), tag the **bottom-20% entropy**
days as the low-entropy regime (expanding quantile, no look-ahead), and compare forward
1/5/21-day SPY returns in low- vs high-entropy days with a HAC (Newey-West) t and a stationary
block-bootstrap null. Offline & deterministic apart from the one cached SPY pull; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — SPY (public, no key) |
| Window | 1995-01-04 → 2026-06-18 (**7,917** return days; **31.5** years) |
| Entropy clock | causal **permutation entropy**, 60-day window, embedding m=3, normalised [0,1] |
| Regime split | **bottom-20%** entropy days = "low-entropy / predictable" (expanding quantile) |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; one-way **1 bp** per turn on the long-in-low-entropy rule |

> **The entropy of returns is nearly maxed out.** Over the whole tape the permutation entropy
> sits in **[0.90, 1.00]** with a mean of **0.98** — SPY daily returns are *almost as
> disordered as white noise*, every day. The "low-entropy" regime is therefore only *relatively*
> ordered (bottom quintile of a tight band), which is the first hint that there is very little
> structure to harvest. **1,513** of 7,917 days (19%) fall in the low-entropy bucket.

## The signal — forward SPY returns in low- vs high-entropy days

1-day entry lag; the gap is low-entropy mean minus high-entropy mean. The **HAC *t*** is a
Newey-West t of the per-day low-vs-high contribution (corrects for overlap + clustering); the
**block-bootstrap *p*** resamples the regime labels in 21-day blocks and asks how often a
clustered random label set produces a gap this large (two-sided).

| horizon | n low | n high | low mean | high mean | gap | low win | base win | HAC *t* | boot *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-day  | 1513 | 6403 | +0.053% | +0.049% | **+0.004%** | 54% | 54% | **0.17** | 0.882 |
| 5-day  | 1513 | 6399 | +0.277% | +0.232% | **+0.045%** | 58% | 59% | **0.44** | 0.735 |
| 21-day | 1513 | 6383 | +1.401% | +0.902% | **+0.499%** | 67% | 66% | **2.05** | 0.300 |

Read it carefully. At **1 and 5 days** there is essentially **nothing** — the low-entropy gap
is a few tenths of a basis point, the win-rate is *at or below* the base rate, and the HAC *t*
is far under 1. Only at **21 days** does a ~0.5pp gap appear with a HAC *t* of **2.05** — but
the block-bootstrap *p* is **0.30**: once you account for the fact that low-entropy days arrive
in long clusters (so the "1,513 observations" are nowhere near 1,513 independent draws), a
random clustered label set beats this gap **30% of the time**. The naive *t* flirts with
significance; the honest, clustering-aware null says it is noise.

## A second entropy measure agrees — there is no clock

Re-running the split on **sample entropy** (Richman-Moorman, 60-day window, m=2) instead of
permutation entropy gives an even weaker picture — the two complexity gauges disagree on
*which* days are "low entropy", and neither finds a payoff:

| horizon | gap | low win | base win | HAC *t* | boot *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-day  | +0.020% | 54% | 54% | 0.63 | 0.504 |
| 5-day  | +0.080% | 58% | 59% | 0.66 | 0.566 |
| 21-day | +0.089% | 65% | 66% | 0.28 | 0.861 |

The 21-day sample-entropy *t* is **0.28** (vs 2.05 for permutation entropy) — the borderline
permutation-entropy number does not even survive a change of estimator. A real regime signal
would not vanish when you swap one entropy formula for another.

## Robustness — the gap is flat-to-noisy in the quantile, and the bootstrap never rejects

21-day horizon; sweep the low-entropy cutoff:

| quantile | n low | 21d gap | HAC *t* | boot *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| bottom 10% | 720 | +0.289% | 0.89 | 0.650 |
| **bottom 20%** | 1513 | +0.499% | 2.05 | 0.300 |
| bottom 30% | 2330 | +0.447% | 2.15 | 0.294 |

The HAC *t* hovers around 2 only because the overlapping-window SE is too small; the
block-bootstrap *p* is **0.29–0.65 at every cutoff** — there is no threshold at which the
clustered null rejects. The "signal" is an artefact of treating autocorrelated, clustered days
as independent observations.

## Tradability — predictable shape, unprofitable strategy

The natural strategy: hold SPY on (lagged) low-entropy days, flat otherwise; charge 1 bp per
turn.

| | annual return | annual Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|
| Low-entropy timing — **gross** | **+1.55%** | **0.20** |
| Low-entropy timing — **net @ 1 bp/turn** | **+1.43%** | **0.19** |
| Buy & hold SPY (same tape) | **+10.63%** | **0.56** |

Exposure is **19%** of days; annual turnover **~11.7×**. Costs barely matter (1 bp shaves
~0.1pp) — the problem is that the rule is **out of the market 81% of the time** and captures a
small slice of the drift at a **worse Sharpe** (0.19 vs 0.56) than simply holding. Timing on
the entropy clock turns a 10.6%/yr buy-and-hold into a 1.4%/yr stub. It is a **MIRAGE** as a
standalone strategy.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and "predictable ≠ profitable"

A deterministic series toggling between a **random** (high sample-entropy) regime and a
**zero-sum cyclic structured** (low sample-entropy) regime. The structured regime is genuinely
more *predictable* (sample entropy ≈ **0.34** vs **1.42**), but by construction its forward
mean equals the random regime's **unless** we plant an edge:

| planted edge | detected low-ent days | regime recall | 5-day gap | HAC *t* | boot *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (predictable, no edge) | 570 | 89% | **−0.06%** | **−0.94** | 0.682 |
| **+0.25%/day** (large edge) | 578 | 89% | **+0.47%** | **+6.30** | 0.011 |

The detector finds the structured regime (**89%** recall), and the inference behaves exactly as
it should: with a more-predictable-but-**no-edge** regime the test stays put (*t* = −0.94, *p* =
0.68) — **low entropy does not manufacture a payoff**; only a real planted edge drives *t* to
6.3 and the bootstrap to *p* = 0.01. The control proves the engine is unbiased **and** isolates
the exact fallacy of the efficiency clock: *predictability of shape is not expected return*.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** On SPY the low-entropy regime's forward-return edge is **null at 1–5 days**
  (win-rate at/below base) and only **borderline at 21 days** (HAC *t* = 2.05) — and that lone
  number **fails the honest clustering-aware test** (block-bootstrap *p* = 0.30), **does not
  survive a switch to sample entropy** (*t* = 0.28), and is flat across quantile cutoffs.
  Literature interest + a non-robust point estimate ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL (the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar
  is not robustly met).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Long-in-low-entropy earns **+1.43%/yr net at Sharpe 0.19** vs
  **+10.63%/yr at Sharpe 0.56** for buy-and-hold. Costs are negligible; the killer is that the
  rule sits out 81% of days and harvests drift at a worse Sharpe. No deployable edge.
- **Predictable = profitable? — BUSTED.** The whole pitch conflates *predictability of shape*
  with *expected return*. The synthetic control makes the gap explicit: a far-more-predictable
  (low-entropy) regime with **zero** planted edge pays **nothing** (*t* = −0.94). Markets sit so
  close to maximum entropy (mean 0.98) that the "clock" barely moves, and where it moves it does
  not pay. Same regime question, different lens as **[Study 397 (Hurst Regime)](../397-hurst-regime/)**.
